processing: Orthodox and CTC black teas alongside small-batch speciality lots, with an emphasis on hand work in the speciality range; the estate also makes dark tea.
harvest_season: Exact picking calendars vary by lot and are rarely stated; speciality teas are usually sold with their own batch details.
appearance_dry: Ranges by grade, from dark whole or broken orthodox leaf to fine CTC granules.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber in the orthodox black teas, darker and more opaque in breakfast grades.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf in the orthodox grades.
taste_profile: Described by tea writer Henrietta Lovell as deep yet elegant with a sweetness recalling fine Chinese tea; the breakfast grades are bolder and made to take milk.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western style. Orthodox lots are worth trying without milk first; breakfast grades take it well.

vintage_note: Mostly sold as current production without a stated vintage, labelled by grade and number such as OP1 or TSFBOP1. Speciality lots are small and change from year to year, and dark tea is the one style here that may be kept for longer.
description:
Satemwa is a family-run estate in Thyolo, in southern Malawi, and one of the last independent farms in a country where agribusiness dominates tea. It stands out for making both everyday breakfast tea and small speciality lots that you do not usually expect from Africa.

The gardens sit at about 1,000 to 1,200 metres. The range covers orthodox grades, a breakfast tea and a dark tea, and the estate favours skilled hand work over machines for its speciality leaf. It also grows coffee and herbs such as hibiscus and lemongrass.

The orthodox teas are the ones to try plain, since they carry more sweetness than the word Malawi leads most people to expect. The breakfast tea is built differently and is happiest with milk.

Look for the grade and number on the label, because the name Satemwa alone covers very different teas. Blends elsewhere may use its leaf too, so check whether a packet is single estate.
history:
The estate's founder was the Scot Maclean Kay. Accounts date its oldest tea fields to 1923 and its oldest surviving bushes to 1926.

Alex Kay now manages the estate and drives its experiments with varieties and processing. The old family home, Huntingdon House, built around 1935, is now a guest house.
